seo.title: 27 Script and Cursive Logos Explained
seo.description: 27 famous script and cursive logos explained by a brand designer: signatures, Spencerian scripts and casual lettering from Coca-Cola, Kellogg's and Disney to Cadbury and Barbie.

intro:
A script logo writes the brand name in joined, handwritten letters, as if someone signed it with a pen. Coca-Cola, Kellogg's, Disney and Cadbury all use one. Script logos feel personal, warm and a little old-fashioned, which is exactly why some of the oldest brands in the world still use them.

Logo design quick course: this guide is part of my series on logo types. Read the others on pictorial marks, combination marks, emblem logos, mascot logos, wordmark logos, monogram logos, lettermark logos, abstract logos, symmetry and negative space, or start with the overview of all types of logos.

What is a script logo?

A script logo is a type of wordmark: the name is the whole logo, with no separate symbol. What makes it a script is the lettering. The letters lean, flow and usually connect, like cursive handwriting. People also call them cursive logos or signature logos.

Most famous script logos are drawn by hand, not typed in a font. Coca-Cola, Kellogg's and Ford were lettered by a person, then cleaned up over the years. That is why each one looks unique, while a logo typed in a popular script font can look like a wedding invitation.

Where script logos come from

Before typewriters, every business letter, invoice and receipt was written by hand. In 19th-century America, schools taught Spencerian script, an elegant slanted handwriting developed by Platt Rogers Spencer, and clear, beautiful penmanship was a sign of a serious business.

So when Coca-Cola's bookkeeper Frank Mason Robinson wrote the drink's name in 1886, he wrote it in Spencerian script. Within twenty years, Campbell's, Ford and Kellogg's had script logos too. Some came from a founder's real signature, which worked like a personal guarantee on the package.

Three types of script logos

Signature scripts: Kellogg's, Disney, Campbell's and Tim Hortons began as a real person's signature. They say: a real person stands behind this product.

Formal scripts: Coca-Cola, Ford, Cartier and Harrods use elegant, carefully drawn lettering with thick and thin strokes. They feel classic, established and premium.

Casual scripts: Instagram, Wendy's, Barbie and Krispy Kreme use bold, relaxed lettering. They feel friendly, fun and approachable.

The problem with script logos: readability

Scripts are the hardest logos to read. Joined letters, loops and thin strokes look beautiful on a shop sign and turn into a scribble on a favicon or a business card. Bold scripts like Kleenex survive at small sizes. Thin signatures like Christian Louboutin's do not.

Readability is also why brands drop their scripts. Johnson & Johnson retired its 130-year-old signature in 2023 for a plain wordmark. Pinterest replaced its script wordmark with a sans serif and kept only the script P in its icon. When Instagram redrew its script in 2026, many users read the new name as "Instagzam". If you choose a script, plan a simple backup mark, like a monogram, for small sizes.

Below are 27 famous script logos, American brands first and then the rest of the world, across food, drinks, fashion, retail, sport, tech and entertainment. Each one has a slide with my handwritten notes and a short explanation.

logoResearch.name: Kellogg's
logoResearch.verifiedFact: W.K. Kellogg signed early boxes of Corn Flakes around 1906, and the red script logo grew out of that signature.
observations: A bold red script with a long flourish on the K.
It reads like a promise from the founder, which is why he signed every box.

logoResearch.name: Disney
logoResearch.verifiedFact: The Disney script is a stylised version of Walt Disney's signature, and Disney says it does not know which artists drew it.
observations: Rounded letters start with a large, open D.
It looks hand-signed, yet Walt's own signature looked different.

logoResearch.name: Campbell's
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Campbell's adopted its red and white label in 1898, and the company says the script was based on founder Joseph Campbell's signature.
observations: Heavy red letters with tall loops on the C and the two Ls.
The script sits on every can, so the logo and the product look the same.

logoResearch.name: Johnson & Johnson
logoResearch.verifiedFact: The script came from co-founder James Wood Johnson's signature on the company's first cheque in 1886, and J&J retired it in 2023.
observations: Two red Johnsons are joined by a tiny ampersand.
The company kept the script for more than 130 years before switching to a plain wordmark.

logoResearch.name: Stüssy
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Shawn Stussy scrawled his surname on the surfboards he made in Laguna Beach in the early 1980s, and it became the logo.
observations: Rough marker strokes run in sharp, uneven lines.
It looks like graffiti, which turned a surfboard signature into a streetwear icon.

logoResearch.name: Tim Hortons
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Hockey player Tim Horton co-founded the chain in Hamilton, Ontario, in 1964, and the logo began as his signature.
observations: A red script runs on one line with tall capitals T and H.
The handwritten name makes a huge coffee chain feel like a local shop.

logoResearch.name: Cadbury
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Cadbury's script is based on the signature of William Cadbury, grandson of founder John Cadbury, and was introduced in 1921.
observations: A gold script opens with a big looping C.
Cadbury redrew it in 2020 to look closer to the original signature.

logoResearch.name: Virgin
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Calligrapher Ray Kyte drew Virgin's signature-style logo in 1978, though the story that it began on a napkin is disputed.
observations: A red handwritten word starts with a V shaped like a tick.
It looks scribbled, which suits a brand that sells itself on breaking the rules.

logoResearch.name: Christian Louboutin
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Christian Louboutin opened his first boutique in Paris in 1991.
observations: A loose black signature with a huge looping L.
The red sole carries the brand, and the signature adds the designer's own hand.

logoResearch.name: Coca-Cola
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Bookkeeper Frank Mason Robinson wrote the name in Spencerian script in 1886, and the logo has kept that style ever since.
observations: Two capital Cs swing into long flourishes.
The script has barely changed in more than 130 years.

logoResearch.name: Ford
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Chief engineer Childe Harold Wills created the Ford script around 1906; it is not a copy of Henry Ford's signature.
observations: A white script with a swash on the F sits inside a blue oval.
Most people assume it is Henry Ford's signature, which is why it feels personal.

logoResearch.name: Budweiser
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Adolphus Busch and Carl Conrad introduced Budweiser in 1876.
observations: An ornate white script with a big B sits on a red bowtie.
The bowtie and the script echo the shape of the old bottle label.

logoResearch.name: Hallmark
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Hallmark trademarked its crown and script logo in 1950, after a staff artist drew it.
observations: A purple script sits under a small five-point crown.
The crown and the script promise quality, which suits a greeting card company.

logoResearch.name: Kleenex
logoResearch.verifiedFact: The Kleenex trademark dates from 1925, and its script has been refined many times since.
observations: Heavy blue letters bounce like a soft tissue.
The script has to stay readable on the narrow side of a tissue box.

logoResearch.name: Dodgers
logoResearch.verifiedFact: The Dodgers' blue script first appeared in 1938, when the team still played in Brooklyn.
observations: A slanted blue script with a red baseball flying off the top.
Speed lines behind the ball make the script look like a home run.

logoResearch.name: Harrods
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Minale Tattersfield created the Harrods logotype in 1967, based on a script hand-drawn by a lettering artist.
observations: Tall, condensed letters start with a strong H.
Printed in gold on green bags, the script doubles as a London souvenir.

logoResearch.name: Cartier
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Louis-François Cartier took over a Paris jewellery workshop in 1847.
observations: Thin and thick strokes look as if they were written with a pen nib.
The script looks handwritten but stays elegant, which suits a jeweller.

logoResearch.name: Milka
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Suchard launched Milka in 1901 in a lilac wrapper.
observations: A rounded lilac script with a tall k.
The letters look poured, which hints at milk chocolate.

logoResearch.name: Instagram
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Instagram redrew its wordmark in August 2026, the first change in 10 years.
observations: The new letters mix handwriting and print, with a joined n and s.
Some users read it as Instagzam, which shows how easily scripts lose clarity.

logoResearch.name: Wendy's
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Wendy's replaced its old serif wordmark with a handwritten-style script in 2013.
observations: A red, casual script sits below the portrait of Wendy.
The relaxed letters make a fast-food chain feel homemade.

logoResearch.name: Chick-fil-A
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Truett Cathy opened the first Chick-fil-A restaurant in an Atlanta mall in 1967.
observations: The C of Chick doubles as a chicken head.
The red script feels friendly, like a hand-painted sign.

logoResearch.name: Krispy Kreme
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Vernon Rudolph started making doughnuts in Winston-Salem, North Carolina, in 1937, and the bowtie was trademarked in 1955.
observations: A red script sits in a green bowtie with DOUGHNUTS below.
The script feels warm and old-fashioned, like a diner sign.

logoResearch.name: Lay's
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Lay's has used a red ribbon over a yellow sun since 1995, and PepsiCo refreshed the logo in 2025.
observations: White script letters sit on a red ribbon.
The sun and ribbon turn the script into a badge that stands out on the bag.

logoResearch.name: Barbie
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Mattel launched Barbie in 1959 with a pink cursive logo.
observations: Bright pink letters with tall, loopy ascenders.
The colour is so tied to the brand that people call it Barbie pink.

logoResearch.name: Vimeo
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Jake Lodwick and Zach Klein launched Vimeo in 2004 while working at CollegeHumor.
observations: A lowercase blue script with joined letters.
The relaxed script makes a video platform feel creative rather than corporate.

logoResearch.name: Fender
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Fender used a thin spaghetti script in the 1950s, then a bolder logo drawn by Robert Perine from the mid-1960s.
observations: A bold script with a sweeping F and a long tail.
It sits on the guitar headstock, so it works as a badge on the instrument.

logoResearch.name: Ray-Ban
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Bausch & Lomb launched Ray-Ban in 1937 to make sunglasses for American pilots.
observations: A white hand-lettered script sits inside a red box.
The box keeps the script readable on the narrow arm of a pair of glasses.

listIntro: The boards below show all 27 script logos in one consistent format, grouped into signatures, formal scripts and casual scripts.
Each logo is reviewed for its design decisions, not for the size or success of the company behind it.
sectionIntroductions: These logos began as a real person's signature, or were drawn to look like one. They put a human name and a human hand on the product.
Formal scripts use elegant lettering with thick and thin strokes, often based on 19th-century penmanship. They feel classic, established and premium.
Casual scripts are bold, relaxed and friendly. They work for food, toys, social apps and lifestyle brands that want to feel approachable.
sectionBridge: This is a visual study of script logos, not a ranking of companies.
Look at how each script joins its letters, how bold the strokes are and how well the name reads at a glance.
entryFallbacks: The script makes the name feel handwritten and personal.
Notice how the logo would read on a sign, a package and a phone screen.

findings.heading: A signature is a promise
findings.text: Kellogg's, Campbell's and Johnson & Johnson used a founder's signature as a personal guarantee of quality.

findings.heading: Custom beats a font
findings.text: Coca-Cola, Ford and Harrods are drawn by hand, so no one else can type the same logo.

findings.heading: Bold scripts survive
findings.text: Kleenex, Wendy's and Lay's use thick strokes, so they still read on small packs and screens.

findings.heading: Scripts love packaging
findings.text: Coca-Cola, Cadbury, Milka and Campbell's look best on cans, bars and wrappers, where the logo is large.

findings.heading: Readability wins in the end
findings.text: Johnson & Johnson and Pinterest dropped their scripts, and Instagram's 2026 redraw shows how easily a script can be misread.

logoRosterConfig.checklistHeading: A practical checklist for a script logo
checklistItems: Can someone read the name in one second?
Is it custom-drawn, not typed in a popular script font?
Do the letters connect without creating confusing shapes?
Does it still work at 24 pixels and in one colour?
Do you have a simple backup mark for icons and social media?
logoRosterConfig.conclusionHtml:
How to design a script logo

1. Pick a style. Decide between a signature, a formal script and a casual script. A law firm and a doughnut shop need very different handwriting.

2. Draw the word. Write the name by hand many times, with a pen, a brush or a marker. A script font is a good starting point for ideas, but the final logo should be drawn, so it belongs only to you.

3. Fix the joins. Clean up how the letters connect, balance the loops and make sure every letter is easy to recognise. Watch for letter pairs that can be misread, like r and z in the new Instagram wordmark.

4. Test it small. Check the logo at 24 pixels, in one colour and on a business card. If the loops fill in, make the strokes bolder or design a simple backup mark for small sizes.

Want a script logo that feels personal?

A great script logo looks like it was written by a real person and still reads at a glance. It is custom-drawn, bold enough for small sizes and paired with a simple backup mark. Coca-Cola, Kellogg's and Disney prove that the right handwriting can last for more than a century.

faq.question: What is a script logo?
faq.answer: A script logo is a wordmark written in joined, handwritten-style letters, like cursive. The name is the whole logo, as in Coca-Cola, Kellogg's, Disney and Cadbury.

faq.question: What is the difference between a script logo and a cursive logo?
faq.answer: They are the same thing. Script is the design term and cursive is the everyday word. A signature logo is a script logo based on a real person's signature, like Kellogg's or Tim Hortons.

faq.question: Can I use a script font for my logo?
faq.answer: You can start with one, but check the font licence and make the logo your own. The most famous script logos are custom-drawn, so no one else can type the same name in the same way.

faq.question: Are script logos hard to read?
faq.answer: They can be. Thin, loopy scripts lose their shape at small sizes. Choose bold strokes, keep the name short and add a simple backup mark, like a monogram, for icons and social media.

faq.question: How much does a script logo cost?
faq.answer: Prices range from a few hundred dollars for a template to tens of thousands with a large agency. I design a complete brand identity, including custom script lettering and a backup mark, in one week for a flat $3,000.
